topic: Philosophy of Religion: Philosophical Issues & Questions
subject: religious-studies

items.title: Wittgenstein's later work treated religious language as a 'language game'
items.claim: How did the later Wittgenstein approach religious language?

options.text: He argued religious language is meaningless

Religious language is a 'language game' embedded in a 'form of life' — it has its own grammar and logic, not reducible to scientific or empirical assertion. It is meaningful within its practice, regardless of whether it asserts external facts
He defended a literal cognitive interpretation
He treated all language games as equally true

items.reveal:
Wittgenstein's 'Philosophical Investigations' (published 1953) replaced the picture theory of meaning from his earlier 'Tractatus' (1921) with a use-theory. 'The meaning of a word is its use in the language.'

Religious language games — prayer, worship, doctrinal assertion — function differently from scientific language games. D.Z. Phillips and Norman Malcolm developed Wittgensteinian philosophy of religion in the 20th century.

Critics (Antony Flew, 'Theology and Falsification' 1950) argued this 'reduces' religious claims to non-cognitive expressions — but Wittgenstein himself was more nuanced, refusing both literalist and reductionist readings.
items.why: The 20th-century philosophy of religion shifted from 'do these claims correspond to reality?' to 'what kind of claims are these?'. Wittgenstein's move opens space for religious practice without requiring scientific-style verification.

items.title: Aquinas offered five arguments for God, not one

options.text: Five distinct arguments from observation: motion (unmoved mover), causation (uncaused cause), contingency (necessary being), degree (greatest being), teleology (designer) — in Summa Theologiae I.2.3

items.reveal:
Aquinas distinguishes 'a priori' arguments (from concept to existence — Anselm's ontological) from 'a posteriori' arguments (from observation). His Five Ways are all a posteriori — they begin from empirical features of the world.

First Way (motion): things move and change; an unmoved mover is required to start the chain. Second Way (efficient causation): everything has a cause; a first cause is required. Third Way (contingency): contingent things require a necessary being. Fourth Way (degree): degrees of perfection require a maximum. Fifth Way (teleology): purposive ordering requires a designer.

Each has been criticised individually. Hume and Kant attacked the cosmological framework; Darwinian biology challenges the teleological reading; Russell's response to Copleston challenged the contingency argument.
items.why: Aquinas is sometimes reduced to a single 'cosmological argument'. He offered five distinct arguments that need to be evaluated separately — and Catholic natural theology still rests on this framework.

items.title: Anselm's ontological argument is a priori

options.text: An empirical argument from observation of nature
God is 'that than which no greater can be conceived'; existence in reality is greater than existence in the mind alone; therefore the greatest conceivable being must exist in reality
A historical argument from biblical events

items.reveal:
Anselm wrote the Proslogion (1077-78) as a contemplation aimed at finding 'a single argument' to prove God's existence. The famous formula appears in Proslogion 2.

Gaunilo (Anselm's contemporary) objected with his 'lost island' parody: by the same logic, the greatest conceivable island must exist. Anselm replied that the argument applies only to a necessary being, not contingent ones.

Descartes (Meditations V), Spinoza, Leibniz and Hegel reformulated versions. Kant's critique — existence is not a predicate (Critique of Pure Reason, 1781) — is the standard counter. Alvin Plantinga's modal version (1974) revived the argument using possible-world semantics.
items.why: The ontological argument is uniquely controversial. Almost everyone has the intuition that something is wrong with it — but the precise diagnosis (Gaunilo's? Kant's? Modal logic?) is itself contested philosophy.
